result:
The sequence starts in [login-form.tsx](src/app/(auth)/login/login-form.tsx). When the form is submitted, it parses the email, password, and “Keep me signed in” checkbox with `loginSchema`, then calls the server action `loginAction`. The server parses the input again; the client-side check only provides quick field feedback.

In [login.ts](src/actions/auth/login.ts), `loginAction` charges the anonymous `auth:login` rate-limit bucket, then calls `AuthService.login` in [auth-service.ts](src/server/services/auth-service.ts). That service charges the same bucket again. It looks up the lowercased email with `userRepository.findUserByEmail`, reads the stored password hash with `findPasswordHash`, and checks the password with `verifyPassword`. `verifyPassword` in [hash.ts](src/lib/hash.ts) derives a scrypt key and compares it in constant time. Missing users and incorrect passwords produce the same credentials error.

On success, `AuthService.login` calls `createSessionToken` in [session-service.ts](src/server/services/session-service.ts). That function generates a random 32-byte token, hashes it with SHA-256, sets an expiry 30 days in the future, and asks `sessionRepository.createSession` in [session-repository.ts](src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts) to store a session row containing the user ID, token hash, expiry, and a null `activeOrgId`. The raw token is not stored in the database.

Back in `loginAction`, `resolveSession(token)` reloads the session and produces a `SessionPrincipal`—user ID, email, active organization ID, and expiry. `setSessionCookie` in [session.ts](src/lib/session.ts) puts the raw token in the `taskflow_session` cookie, marked `httpOnly`, `sameSite: "lax"`, path `/`, and secure in production. The action returns the principal to the form as its result; it does not return the token or password hash. When the form sees success, it navigates to the `next` path. The checkbox is parsed, but the session lifetime does not vary with it: sessions are always issued for 30 days.

For a later request, [proxy.ts](src/proxy.ts) checks only whether the cookie exists. If it does not, it redirects to `/login`; if it does, the proxy lets the request continue. That check is only a quick gate, not proof that the session is valid. Server code calls `getSessionPrincipal` in [session.ts](src/lib/session.ts): it reads the cookie, hashes its token through `resolveSession`, and looks up the matching session and user in the repository. The repository rejects missing or expired sessions, and `getSessionPrincipal` also checks the expiry against the current time. A missing, unknown, or expired token resolves to `null`.

After sign-in, the usual `next` destination is the organization chooser, `/orgs`. Its page in [orgs/page.tsx](src/app/(dashboard)/orgs/page.tsx) gets the principal and lists the user’s organizations; if there is only one, it redirects straight to that organization’s slug. The principal establishes identity, but it has no role. For a workspace URL, [the `[orgSlug]` layout](src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/layout.tsx) gets the principal, resolves the organization, and calls `resolveActorForOrg` in [session-service.ts](src/server/services/session-service.ts). That function finds the organization by slug, loads the user’s active membership, and builds an `Actor` containing the user ID, organization ID, and membership role. Missing or inactive membership does not produce an actor. The layout checks the organization scope and passes the actor into the workspace tree.

The layout also gathers workspace data and renders `DashboardShell` in [dashboard-shell.tsx](src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/_components/dashboard-shell.tsx). It passes the actor to `AppSidebar` in [app-sidebar.tsx](src/components/domain/nav/app-sidebar.tsx). The sidebar filters the navigation declared in [nav.ts](src/config/nav.ts): `visibleNav` checks each item’s permission with `can()` and applies any feature-flag gate. `can()` in [permissions.ts](src/lib/permissions.ts) first enforces that the actor and resource belong to the same organization, then applies the role matrix (and any ownership rules). The resulting `Actor` is also the identity-and-role context used by server actions and services to authorize workspace operations; hiding a sidebar link is not the authorization check for those operations.
